To address these challenges simultaneously, we propose a new framework of trusted collaborator group formation and the supporting resource allocation strategy for concurrent task orchestration. Specifically, a collaborative task is decomposed into subtasks subject to dynamic resource availability and inter-subtask dependencies. A task utility model is developed for collaborator group evaluation support subtask allocation according to task completion goals and unified value-risk analysis. Based on this model, concurrent task orchestration is formulated as a long-term utility maximization problem under α-fairness. To solve the problem efficiently, we develop a hierarchical matching strategy that first clusters tasks and collaborators into coarse-grained sets and subsequently performs fine-grained collaborator group formation and task allocation within matched sets. Task-specific trust is predicted through spatial-temporal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and embedded into a fairness-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework to continuously update the matching policies. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy improves concurrent task completion performance by 22% over representative baselines under resource constraints.

papers.title: Tiny Recursive Policy: Recursive Latent Refinement for Visuomotor Control
papers.authors: Hakan Aktas, Cengiz Oztireli
papers.summary: Behaviour cloning has become a powerful approach for robotic manipulation, but many modern policies reconstruct their internal representation from a fixed observation window at each prediction and do not maintain persistent latent context throughout execution. We introduce Tiny Recursive Policy (TRP), a parameter-efficient behaviour-cloning policy that combines persistent temporal state with recursive latent refinement. At each control step, TRP repeatedly updates high- and low-level latent states using a shared computation module before decoding an action sequence, and propagates the resulting state to subsequent predictions. We evaluate TRP across LIBERO-100, MetaWorld ML45, and the LIBERO-Mem benchmarks. TRP performs competitively across multi-task and few-shot settings and shows substantial gains on long-horizon and context-dependent tasks, while using significantly fewer parameters than large generative baselines. Execution-time perturbations show that reliance on the persistent carry increases with temporal-context demand, while training with carry perturbations substantially improves robustness to both carry and visual corruptions. Ablations reveal a strong interaction between persistent state and recursive refinement: the benefit of carry depends strongly on the amount of within-step computation, and the resulting performance cannot be explained by parameter count alone.

papers.title: LooseLeaf: Enabling Serverless GPUs for Computational Notebooks
papers.authors: Yusen Wu, Tingfeng Lan, Benjamin Carver, Haoliang Wang et al.
papers.summary: Computational notebooks reserve a GPU for the whole session, yet the GPU computes only while a cell executes and sits idle otherwise. Serverless execution would release the GPU between cells, but reconstructing the accumulated notebook state on a fresh worker imposes substantial cost on every GPU cell. This paper presents LooseLeaf, a serverless GPU platform for interactive notebooks. LooseLeaf derives the state and import closures of each cell, the minimal variables and packages that the cell needs. Our analysis on 5,000 real-world notebooks shows that these closures are small, and user-cell editing leaves seconds to prepare them. LooseLeaf prepares a GPU worker with these closures while the user edits the cell. After execution, the worker saves the updated state within seconds, so the GPU is reclaimable after every cell. LooseLeaf starts 95-98% of GPU cells with no visible delay, matches the interactivity of a pinned session, and provisions 32-55% fewer GPU-hours than state-of-the-art notebook platforms.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
papers.authors: Himani Sinhmar, Vaibhav Srivastava, Naomi Ehrich Leonard
papers.summary: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability. NDD makes safe-and-live deconfliction a controllable, locally tunable emergent property of local agent interactions, without requiring communication, preassigned priorities, models of neighbors' objectives or future actions, or estimates of group size or global network properties. By design, NDD couples the dynamics of internal decision and attention states with changing physical states and locally observed relative motion. Each agent continuously modulates its speed along its prescribed path, responding as soon and as much as conflict resolution requires. Agents self-organize into disjoint, locally engaged groups that resolve conflicts concurrently. When any group's conflict becomes safety-critical, decision-action feedback destabilizes collective indecision, and coordinated conflict-resolution emerges that stabilizes a safe traversal order within the group. Order persists as conflicts clear, but groups may split or merge as agents autonomously adapt to new conflicts and those with resolved conflicts resume their nominal motion. We derive explicit conditions on sensing range, feedback gains, response time scales, and actuation limits that guarantee collision avoidance and traversal-order formation in finite time with no deadlock or livelock for finite, heterogeneous agent populations of arbitrary, changing size. Computational cost scales with the number of local interactions sensed by each agent. Large-scale simulations, comparisons with existing approaches, and hardware experiments demonstrate NDD in complex congested scenarios and validate its scalability.

papers.title: Operationalizing Governed Agentic Workflows in Regulated Finance: A Customer Zero Case Study using Zafin AIOS
papers.authors: Shahir Daya, Rob Dunlap, Alexandre Boulenger, Ahmed Abdelmoneim et al.
papers.summary: Regulated industries such as finance and healthcare face critical governance challenges that hamper the adoption of AI-assisted software development and hinder the transition from experimental pilots to production work. This paper presents Zafin AIOS, an end-to-end orchestration platform and control plane designed to deploy AI within regulated industries such as finance. We provide the architectural principles and an empirical comparison between AI-assisted and human-led workloads. To validate this framework empirically, we conduct a case study analysis of Zafin's internal enterprise workflows, which we refer to as Customer Zero. This paper contributes a production case study of AI-assisted software engineering in regulated industries. We evaluate the results of using Zafin AIOS with two different production codebases, one for the pricing execution platform and the other for the client deal negotiation platform. Our contribution is a customer case study for regulated industries with production codebases and governance, which includes proof of work. The results demonstrate that strictly governed agentic orchestration increases enterprise capacity without compromising control. In the pricing execution platform workflows, the platform provided complete observability and reduced effort by 38%. In the client deal negotiation platform, it reduced reporting work by 76% while maintaining all predefined data privacy, role-based access, and audit guardrails. This paper bridges the gap between AI-assisted software engineering theory and the operational reality of compliance. Closing this gap is important to help enterprises take advantage of AI technologies. These results are descriptive of the benefits of using governed workflows in regulated industries.

papers.title: ORBIT: A Modular Multi-finger Robotic Hand Platform with Rotational Finger Reconfiguration
papers.authors: Benito Ribadeneira, Siqi Shang, Lillian Chin
papers.summary: Despite the popularity of multi-fingered robotic hands for dexterous manipulation, there is no systematic platform to compare different hand morphologies against one another. We present ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand), a modular platform designed to enable principled exploration of multi-fingered hand morphology. The core contribution of ORBIT is a rotating knuckle mechanism, where independent fingers travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive. This enables ORBIT to perform quick recon- figuration (< 1 s) of finger layout without hand disassembly. ORBITs a robust system, with finger average angular velocity of 1.57 rad / s1 and a root finger force resistance of 50 N. Using a three fingers instantiation of ORBIT, we demonstrate an initial pilot grasping study, comparing anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style finger layouts across eleven objects of varied size, shape, and texture. We further demonstrate how ORBITs nonanthropomorphic orbital DOF enables the achievement of tasks that would be difficult to perform with fixed-knuckle designs, such as cube face reorientation, lid threading, and precision pinching of sub-centimeter objects. These results establish ORBIT as a viable platform for direct apples to apples comparison of multi-fingered hand morphologies for specific manipulation tasks

papers.title: Alignment of Autonomous Cyber Defense Agents via Adaptive Policy Shaping
papers.authors: Dena Mujtaba, Bharadwaj Ravichandran, Brian Hu, Arslan Basharat
papers.summary: Cybersecurity operators increasingly encounter sophisticated and fast-paced attacks, making autonomous cyber defense (ACD) a critical approach for supporting timely and effective decision-making. Reinforcement learning (RL)-based ACD agents have the ability to autonomously observe network states and take actions to defend and recover system assets, making them well suited for ACD. However, these agents often face critical trade-offs, such as improving network security while inadvertently degrading service availability or violating other operational priorities such as confidentiality and integrity, raising the core challenge of aligning agent behavior with human-specified goals and intent. In this work, we study the problem of aligning RL-based ACD agents with human-specified operational objectives without requiring costly retraining. We formalize alignment for ACD as a policy shaping problem, where a pretrained RL decision-making policy can be adjusted at test time using predicted attributes over agent actions. We also propose an adaptive approach that dynamically controls the alignment–performance trade-off as operational priorities shift during an ongoing cyber attack. We evaluate our method in a simulated cyber defense environment, CybORG, analyzing performance across multiple alignment objectives using the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) information security triad. Our results show that adaptive test-time policy shaping can significantly improve alignment while preserving core cyber defense performance, offering a practical and scalable alternative to training-time alignment methods in RL. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ITM-Kitware/alignment-cage-challenge-2.

papers.title: CCAaaS: An Orchestration Platform for High-Velocity Design, Development, and Deployment of Data Center Transports at Meta
papers.authors: Prankur Gupta, Balasubramanian Madhavan, Miao Xu, Prashanth Kannan et al.
papers.summary: Today, data center networks run multiple congestion control algorithms (CCAs), each tailored to distinct traffic characteristics, from latency-sensitive intra-region RPCs to high-throughput cross-region AI workloads. The rapid evolution of AI training and inference further accelerates this trend by continually introducing new traffic characteristics that demand new CCAs. This paper introduces CCA-as-a-Service (CCAaaS), our eBPF-based ecosystem for the rapid design, deployment, and operation of production-grade CCAs at hyperscale. We present (1) a modular BPF-TCP framework and general lessons for designing modular CCAs; (2) a deployment and orchestration layer that provides disruption-free CCA updates, along with best practices for managing a zoo of CCAs at scale; and (3) a lightweight observability tool for CCAs and a blueprint for scaling CCA observability. CCAaaS manages over 97% of our server-to-server traffic using three active eBPF-based CCAs; two of the five CCAs we have built have since been deprecated. We show that our eBPF-centric approach to CCAs development delivers the same application-level performance (retransmissions, bandwidth, and tail latency) as their native in-kernel counterparts, and that our custom CCAs add negligible CPU and memory cost over their eBPF baselines. In terms of realized benefits, the CCA built with CCAaaS significantly improved network, and application metrics, for example, one of our CCAs reduced P99 latency for cross-region services by up to 20X.

papers.title: Causal-based approaches to explain and learn from self-extension - A review
papers.authors: Rebeca Marfil, Pablo Bustos, Antonio Bandera
papers.summary: The last decades have seen a revolution in autonomous robotics. Deep learning approaches and their hardware implementations have made it possible to endow robots with extraordinary perceptual capabilities. In addition, they can also benefit from advances in Automated Planning, allowing them to autonomously solve complex tasks. However, on many occasions, the robot still acts without internalising and understanding the reasons behind a perception or an action, beyond an immediate response to a current state of the context. This gap results in limitations that affect its performance, reliability and trustworthiness. Deep learning alone cannot bridge this gap, because the reasons behind behaviour, when it emanates from a model in which the world is a black-box, are not accessible. What is really needed is an underlying architecture based on deeper reasoning. Among other issues, this architecture should enable the robot to generate explanations, allowing people to know why the robot is performing, or has performed, a certain action, or the reasons that may have caused a certain plan failure or perceptual anomaly. Furthermore, when these explanations arise from a cognitive process and are shared, and thus validated, with people, the robot should be able to incorporate these explanations into its knowledge base, and thus use this understanding to improve future behaviour. Our article looks at recent advances in the development of self-aware, self-evolving robots. These robots are designed to provide the necessary explanations to their human counterparts, thereby enhancing their functional capabilities, in the quest to gain their trust.

papers.title: Holo-NN: Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search via Compressive Sensing
papers.authors: Bryant Gipson
papers.summary: In the age of AI, privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search over high-dimensional embeddings has emerged as a critical yet frustratingly challenging domain, dominated by tradeoffs between speed, privacy, and accuracy. Traditional tree and graph-based indexing structures (e.g., HNSW, ScaNN) rely fundamentally on non-linear operations that are computationally intractable under Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) or blind server-side constraints. In this paper, we introduce Holo-NN (Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search), an algebraic framework that replaces data-dependent branching with a single linear projection. Our key observation is that while distances across a database are dense, neighborhood membership is inherently sparse: only a handful of points ever lie close to a query. By pairing locality-preserving feature transforms with Compressive Sensing, Holo-NN folds the entire database offline into a compact holographic sensing matrix. At query time, encrypted search reduces to a single, non-interactive matrix-vector multiplication—requiring no FHE bootstrapping, no multi-round interaction, and no client-side index state. This turns private retrieval into an embarrassingly parallel, accuracy-tunable computation that runs out of the box on both CPUs and GPUs, scaling efficiently to production databases. We offer a comparison against other state-of-the-art Private ANN algorithms to help situate the method in the broader context of production-grade private retrieval.

papers.title: A-GE: Privacy-Preserving Age Assurance via Fine-Grained Motion
papers.authors: Mohammed Gharib, Giovanni Cascone, Martin Zizi
papers.summary: Age assurance faces a fundamental privacy dilemma: meaningful assurance typically requires revealing identity or other sensitive information, whereas privacy-preserving alternatives often provide little assurance. Existing approaches either disclose sensitive information directly or shift the disclosure and trust requirement to an identity provider, while self-declared age provides little meaningful assurance. Thus, a fundamental gap remains between establishing an age property and revealing information beyond what is necessary to establish that property. We present A-GE (Age-Grounded Evidence), a privacy-preserving age assurance system that derives age-related evidence from fine-grained motion captured by commodity inertial measurement units (IMUs). A-GE exploits subtle motion dynamics that we hypothesize reflect underlying neuromuscular and physiological processes during ordinary device interaction. It requires neither identity information nor government identification and operates across available sensor sampling rates, including the approximately 60 Hz limit of web-based sensing, with configurable minimum-age thresholds ranging from 14 to 21 years. We evaluate A-GE on more than 600 participants, with separate participant-disjoint cohorts for model development and final evaluation. At a 16-year minimum-age threshold, A-GE achieves up to 93.8% accuracy with a comparable F1 score across the evaluated configurations. We further demonstrate client-side deployment on Android, iOS, and the web, and examine unintended attribute inference and residual privacy risks, characterizing both the privacy benefits and limitations of deriving age evidence from commodity motion.

papers.title: Deletion, Substitution, Repair and Transplant: Component Attribution in BARBICAN, a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for MCP
papers.authors: İpek Abasıkeleş Turgut, Edip Gümüş
papers.summary: A neural classifier can fail completely inside a layered defense without any end-to-end number moving. We demonstrate this on BARBICAN, a fail-closed gateway for language-model tool mediation whose arbitration stage spent an entire recorded evaluation receiving text mangled by a misconfigured tokenizer. Correcting the misconfiguration lifts that stage's corpus-wide area under the ROC curve (AUC) from 0.392 to 0.855 and pushes system recall down, from 80.67% to 80.34%; a stub that answers "malicious" scores 80.77%, higher than either. The reason emerges once the stage's input distribution is examined: upstream routing hands it a band that is 96.82% malicious, and the enforcement design lets an incriminating verdict block while an exculpating one releases an input only through one narrow branch. Yet deleting it costs 673 detections. Substituting its verdict with a constant instead moves between 12 and 140 of 25,000 decisions. Transplanted into the arbitration stage, an off-the-shelf classifier that separates the band's inputs at an AUC of 0.916 changes 16 of 25,000 decisions. Measured against such detectors with operating points chosen away from the test data, the gateway leads on its own benchmark distribution and falls behind once that distribution changes. In our earlier gateway, the review model's band is 92.94% malicious and a constant verdict is as accurate as the review model. We argue that an ablation figure for any routed stage is unreadable without the class balance of the band that stage receives, and that deletion experiments need substitution experiments beside them.

papers.title: Cross-Platform Application Migration to HarmonyOS: An Agentic Pipeline with Artifact-Derived Verification
papers.authors: Ergun Biçici, Mehmet Kaygusuz, Fatih Turan Gündoğdu, Emre Filiz et al.
papers.summary: The migration of applications written for a different platforms like Android or iOS to HarmonyOS NEXT requires a complete rewrite in ArkTS. Although LLMs automate the translation of source constructs into ArkTS, syntactic compilation is not enough and functional assurance is a critical open challenge in HarmonyOS NEXT migration. We present HMOS Migrator, an agentic pipeline that reads an application's source code, generates an ArkTS project, and validates the result by replaying recorded interactions on a real device. We cast the scoring problem as quality estimation without a reference implementation; we score a migration using only the source application's recorded behaviour and the artifacts produced by the pipeline. We define seven weighted metrics, each constructed so that reduced measurement cannot artificially raise the score. Over twelve runs across six open-source applications, the pipeline's structural reproduction is high (completeness 83.3–100.0), while on-device behaviour (4.3–63.1) and UI fidelity (21.1–63.2) remain the primary limits. Scores improve steadily over time: +0.45 points per day overall (R²=0.44, p=0.019) and +0.47 over the model-free subset (R²=0.39, p=0.029), with corresponding to fit angles of +8.4° and +11.7° respectively.

papers.title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
papers.authors: Rachel Poonsiriwong, Pat Pataranutaporn
papers.summary: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? We conducted a randomized experiment (N = 576) comparing four embodied avatars–a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human–with a text chatbot and no-intervention control. All embodied conditions increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to the control (beta = .401-.609, all q <= .0126) and chatbot (beta = .398-.604, all q <= .007), without differing significantly from one another. Only the Beluga condition increased immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. Among 287 returners assessed two months later, following an intermediate assigned-condition session, Beluga also showed significantly higher pre-booster sustainable product choice compared to the control (beta = .657, q = .0176). Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.

papers.title: SEMAC: Spherical Energy Matching Ambisonics Codec for Efficient Higher-Order Ambisonics Compression
papers.authors: Christoph Hold, Jan Buethe, Jean-Marc Valin, Jan Skoglund et al.
papers.summary: Higher-order Ambisonics (HOA) is an attractive format for immersive spatial audio, but its high channel count and directional properties present significant audio coding challenges. The widely deployed Opus audio codec supports HOA through Channel Mapping Families 2 and 3 (RFC 8486), which code and transmit every Ambisonics channel, so the bitrate grows quadratically with the spherical harmonic order. We introduce SEMAC, which instead represents an Ambisonics signal by a quantized full-order directional energy envelope together with fewer CELT-coded transport channels. CELT separates a per-band energy envelope from the signal shape and restores it after quantization, and SEMAC generalizes this principle to directional signals. Since the reduced transport spans only a lower-dimensional subspace, the decoder re-imposes the envelope observed at the encoder input, restoring the directional energy distribution at full order. A MUSHRA test on fifth-order material compares SEMAC against Opus CMF 3 in matched configurations at 512 and 768 kbit/s. SEMAC with 16 of 36 transport channels is rated above full-order CMF 3 at both rates, and at equal transport channel count above order truncation. The proposed SEMAC strategy of coding fewer transport channels with the directional envelope is found perceptually preferable to coding all HOA channels at low precision.

papers.title: WebUniverse: Scaling Verified Training Data for Agentic Web Development
papers.authors: Yaorui Ding, Fengqing Jiang, Yichen Feng, Yuetai Li et al.
papers.summary: Training agents for front-end web development requires demonstrations of code editing, execution, browser inspection and revision, yet public trajectories and reusable task environments remain limited. We introduce WebUniverse, a pipeline that constructs verifiable tasks with verified development trajectories from open-source repositories and real web pages. The tasks cover text-grounded application development in standalone and iterative settings and vision-grounded reproduction across pages and viewports. We collect agent trajectories for these tasks and verify the resulting applications against task-specific functional or visual requirements. We release WebUniverse-Env, containing 15K executable task environments, and WebUniverse-Mix, containing the corresponding 15K development trajectories with verification records and scores. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on WebUniverse-Mix raises the Vision2Web average score from 51.7 to 68.3, WebGen-Bench accuracy from 34.5% to 63.9%, and Web-Bench pass@2 from 12.2% to 23.1%. The resulting model also outperforms a public-data baseline trained with the same configuration and sample budget across all reported metrics. Ablations show complementary benefits from text and visual trajectories and continued gains as training data scales from 5K to 15K trajectories.

papers.title: CoupleFlow: Null-Calibrated Auditory Attention Decoding With Time-Locked Brain-Speech Coupling and Flow-Matching Likelihood Ratios
papers.authors: Ali Alavi, Donald S. Williamson
papers.summary: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) seeks to identify the attended talker from brief noninvasive brain recordings by comparing neural responses with competing speech streams. Recent electroencephalography (EEG) decoders report nearly perfect accuracy from one second of data, yet we show that this performance fails to generalize to unseen speech because models exploit trial leakage, eye gaze, and acoustic cues instead of speech evoked neural activity. We introduce CoupleFlow, which decodes attention through temporal coupling between neural and acoustic embeddings. Its predictions remain at chance when the brain signal contains no informative coupling, preventing shortcuts based on speech content or talker identity. A conditional flow matching head implements a likelihood ratio decision rule based on pointwise mutual information between brain and speech. This rule is Bayes optimal when the recording depends only on the attended talker and removes preferences for speech that is likely a priori. We evaluate CoupleFlow with content disjoint splits recovered from the audio and null tests that distinguish genuine temporal coupling from trial recognition. Across nine EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG) datasets processed through a common pipeline, spanning four languages, high density EEG recordings, listeners with hearing impairment, and a room with multiple talkers, CoupleFlow outperforms linear and deep baselines while all null tests remain at chance. Finally, we derive an evidence accumulation law that predicts accuracy across window lengths from a single parameter per dataset and predicts that parameter from the strength of neural speech tracking. This law identifies recording signal to noise ratio as a limit on decoding speed and reliability and estimates the window length required to reach a target accuracy.

papers.title: What Mean Error Misses: Device-Clock Diagnostics for Evaluating Eye Tracking across Three Virtual Reality Headsets
papers.authors: Aleksandr Chernysh, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Kamrul Hasan, Md Arif Shahriar et al.
papers.summary: Gaze research in virtual reality needs eye trackers of known error. Thirty participants completed the same protocol on the Meta Quest Pro (QP), HTC VIVE Pro Eye (PE) and HTC VIVE Focus Vision (FV); to our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of the FV eye tracker. In a random-saccade task, median participant mean error was 1.04° on QP, 1.50° on PE and 2.41° on FV, which remained least accurate after linear recalibration. In a later block with a darker background, PE error rose by 0.70°. FV samples were positively correlated: dispersion was 9.8 times the sample-to-sample root mean square. The device clocks showed losses that mean error hides. QP paused for up to 6.04 s, and FV skipped single samples. During instructed eye closures, QP flagged every sample valid while gaze moved 9.74°. Evaluations should report repeated timestamps, loss composition on the device clock and validity during eye closures.

papers.title: When Should I Trust This? Designing and Evaluating Factuality Indicators for LLM-based Chatbots
papers.authors: Greta Warren, Jessica Heal, Sila Eser, Denise M. Leto et al.
papers.summary: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

papers.title: Noisy Target Training Meets Drifting for Weakly-Supervised Speech Enhancement
papers.authors: Yoshiki Masuyama, Dominik Klement, Christoph Boeddeker, Julius Richter et al.
papers.summary: In speech enhancement, standard supervised training requires pairs of noisy and clean speech. Such pairs are typically created by artificially degrading clean speech, leading to a domain mismatch between synthetic training data and real recordings. Noisy target training (NyTT) mitigates this limitation by training an enhancement model to predict a noisy recording from a noisier version generated by adding extra noise. However, since the training target is noisy, NyTT might learn to leave residual noise in the enhanced output. In this paper, we address this issue in NyTT by incorporating a Sinkhorn drifting loss that matches the distribution of the enhanced speech to that of unpaired clean speech. The Sinkhorn drifting loss attracts enhanced speech toward high-density regions of the clean-speech distribution while repelling it from the current enhanced-speech distribution in latent space. This loss uses only unpaired clean speech rather than the clean counterpart of each degraded recording, preserving the weakly-supervised nature of NyTT. Experimental results on VoiceBank-DEMAND and CHiME-3 real recordings demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed combination.

papers.title: Beyond pass or fail: an information-processing account of the Turing Test
papers.authors: Qiwei Zhao, Oriana Pansardi, James W. Strachan, Eugenio Scaliti et al.
papers.summary: The Turing Test is passed when a human interrogator cannot distinguish machine-generated responses from human ones. Yet behavioral indistinguishability can reflect two fundamentally different failures: a failure of encoding, in which machine and human output distributions overlap so closely that source information is effectively absent; or a failure of readout, in which source information is present but the interrogator fails to extract it. To dissociate these possibilities, we inverted the Turing Test, placing humans and AI systems in symmetrical interrogator roles. Using a quantitative information-processing framework, we separated encoding, the information contained in the text; readout, the extraction of that information by an interrogator; and meta-readout, the interrogator's explicit access to the features guiding its own judgments. Across two series of experiments involving more than 3800 human interrogators and two generations of GPT models (GPT-4 and GPT-5), we found a striking dissociation across processing levels and interrogator types. As AI-generated responses became more human-like from GPT-4 to GPT-5, source information became more difficult for human interrogators to extract. GPT-5 interrogators, by contrast, read out source-discriminating information more accurately than GPT-4 interrogators. This improvement, however, came with a specific limitation: GPT-5 explanations only partially aligned with the feature weightings that actually predicted their judgments. Human interrogators showed the complementary pattern, with modest readout alignment but comparatively higher meta-readout alignment. Together, these findings suggest a double dissociation between readout and meta-readout across human and GPT interrogators.

papers.title: GlanceAR: Repurposing Phone Sensors via Low-Cost Reflectors for Always-On Obstacle Awareness
papers.authors: Boyang Zhou, Xizhe Hao, Minbeom Kim, Jaewook Lee et al.
papers.summary: Smartphone use while walking reduces environmental awareness and can lead to accidents and injury, yet existing obstacle-awareness systems remain unadopted because they require users to hold the phone upright and aimed forward, conflicting with how people actually hold their devices. We introduce GlanceAR, an always-on mobile obstacle-awareness system designed for natural phone-holding postures. GlanceAR utilizes a low-cost passive mirror attachment to redirect the phone's rear LiDAR and RGB camera forward without additional electronic components. In a within-subjects study with N=11 participants navigating indoor and outdoor obstacle courses while engaged in a primary on-phone task, we evaluated three sensing configurations: GlanceAR, a LiDAR-only variant for privacy, and an attachment-free ultra-wide camera baseline. Our findings reveal trade-offs among sensing fidelity, obstacle cue design, and social acceptability, and surface insights around AI complacency and the tension between on-screen task focus and physical safety.

papers.title: On Latency-Optimal Implementations of the Timestamp Object
papers.authors: Aurojit Panda, Scott Shenker, Sam Toueg, Wen Zhang
papers.summary: Timestamps are widely used in distributed algorithms to order operations. In this paper, we study the timestamp object (TS), which provides a single operation that returns strictly increasing integers. We ask two questions: What is the maximum resilience and the minimum latency of TS implementations in asynchronous message-passing systems, where latency is measured by worst-case message delay? We answer these questions under various types of failure: crash failures, and Byzantine failures with and without digital signatures. To do so, we give lower bounds and algorithms that determine (1) the optimal resilience of TS implementations under each type of failure, and (2) the optimal latency in all cases but one. Along the way, we introduce a new lower-bound proof technique called a cyclic chain argument, which constructs a cycle of indistinguishable schedules along which the returned timestamps must strictly increase, yielding a contradiction.

papers.title: The Cost of a Real Grover Oracle: Minecraft Seed Search from Software to Quantum Hardware
papers.authors: Evan M. Reeves, Elias Sopkin, Thomas A. Searles
papers.summary: We present the resource estimation of how known-constant arithmetic changes the cost of a Grover oracle for Minecraft 1.13.1 seed recovery, an application of quantum search to procedural content generation. The oracle developed here combines a structure-placement predicate with a reversible inverse transform of the linear congruential generator for the 32-bit residual search. Reduced-width arithmetic, phase marking, uncomputation, and complete Grover loops are verified against an independent Java reference, while production-width circuits are structurally audited. Direct Fourier-basis constant arithmetic reduces the placement-predicate width from 6n+3 to 4n+3 qubits and the structural scaling of the two-qubit gate counts from Theta(n³) to O(n²). Under backend-agnostic common-basis Qiskit level-0 u, CX accounting, the representative nonzero-r folded residual-search construction uses 275 circuit qubits, 48,896 CX gates, and depth 4,482, versus 467 qubits, 2,038,804 CX gates, and depth 186,328 for the original register-to-register baseline. Multi-placement conjunctions expose a width-recomputation tradeoff, and exact enumeration identifies a plateau in candidate reduction for the benchmark. We executed reduced-width placement circuits within complete Grover loops on IBM processors and Quantinuum H2-1 and show larger one-iteration increases in marked-state probability for the specialized construction than for the baseline. These results quantify the resource benefits of arithmetic specialization and show substantial routing sensitivity in the reduced-width IBM hardware experiments. Together, the results quantify the effect of specializing known-constant arithmetic within a PCG-derived oracle and show that its compiled hardware behavior strongly depends on routing and execution context.

papers.title: Multi-Timescale Context-Aware Radio Resource Optimization for Harmonious NTN-TN Coexistence: A Digital Twin and Open RAN Enabled Framework
papers.authors: Ecem Izde Kaya, Md. Zoheb Hassan, Georges Kaddoum
papers.summary: Coexistence between non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) and terrestrial networks (TNs) is essential for future wireless systems, but terrestrial downlink transmissions can generate harmful aggregate interference at low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite receivers. We present DT-STABLE, an Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN)-enabled, digital twin (DT)-assisted framework for context-aware NTN-TN coexistence. Using site-specific information, the DT estimates interference at LEO satellites, enabling proactive management with reduced real-time measurement overhead. We formulate joint beam activation and user association under RF-chain limits, load balancing, and aggregate satellite interference constraints; prove NP-hardness; and develop an efficient DT-guided scheduling algorithm. DT-STABLE couples short-timescale radio resource adaptation with periodic mid- and long-timescale DT updates through standardized O-RAN interfaces. Site-specific 28 GHz simulations under worst-case satellite geometry and low elevation angles show that DT-STABLE balances rate and interference utility, achieving 89.63% interference-to-noise ratio (INR) satisfaction and a mean sum rate of 210.96 bps/Hz, with nearly 100% INR satisfaction when satellite protection is prioritized. The framework reduces beam measurement overhead by 99.71% relative to exhaustive sweeping and achieves up to 33.1 times lower runtime than the Gurobi-based exact optimization benchmark.

papers.title: Sounding Surgical Instrument Localisation through Audio-Visual Correspondence
papers.authors: Dominic Behling, Jonas Hein, Matthias Seibold
papers.summary: Surgical scene understanding is a prerequisite for context-aware and intelligent systems in the operating room. Current methods rely mostly on visual data, while acoustic sensing has shown potential to provide complementary information on surgical activity. First approaches for the localisation of surgical activity relied on microphone arrays and acoustic beamforming. This work investigates whether the active instrument can be localized from a single microphone and a camera by learning the correspondence between the appearance and the sound of surgical instruments, without annotating its position. We adapt weakly supervised audio-visual localisation, which learns from the co-occurrence of image and sound, to the surgical setting. We record simulated surgical actions, sawing, drilling, and chiseling, and train the model on these recordings without any spatial annotation to produce a heatmap over the sounding tool. We extend the training objective by two terms: a silence term, which suppresses the output for silence and background noise, and a composite term, which trains the model to select the sounding one of two visible instruments. The model localizes the active instrument on an independent corpus recorded with a different camera and microphone, in which instrument positions were obtained by optical tracking. It separates tool activity from silence and background noise and can attribute sound correctly when two tools are present. Audio-visual correspondence learned from in-domain recordings connects the sound of a surgical action to the instrument that produces it, using a single microphone and a camera. This proof of concept introduces a novel paradigm that enables the detection and localisation of surgical activity without manual annotations.

papers.title: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
papers.authors: Mohammad Mussadiq Jalalzai, Tobias Klenze, Jovan Komatovic
papers.summary: The consensus protocols of most high-performance blockchains use quorum certificates, which bundle the signatures of a quorum of validators. Signature schemes such as BLS can aggregate the signatures of a whole quorum into a single short signature, which keeps these certificates small. A large-scale quantum computer would break these schemes, and no post-quantum scheme with comparable aggregate size and aggregation time is known. Without aggregation, a certificate holds one large post-quantum signature per member of the quorum, so it becomes infeasible for each validator to broadcast certificates, as modern consensus protocols often require. We present Quantum Cadence, a post-quantum consensus protocol with multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates altogether: every validator counts quorums among the messages it has received itself. Its safety and liveness do not even depend on signatures, although we add signatures to obtain accountability. Quantum Cadence builds on Cadence and replaces its slot consensus, Chorus, with Quantum Chorus, which keeps the optimal fast-path latency of Chorus: dissemination followed by two rounds of votes. When its fast path fails, Quantum Chorus runs Coda, our signature-free Byzantine agreement for multiple proposers. We also outline how the Conductor, which schedules the slots of Cadence, can be adapted to Quantum Cadence. In simulations with 200 validators, Quantum Chorus has a latency comparable to that of Chorus and scales better with the number of proposers.

papers.title: Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes
papers.authors: Wendi Sang, Kai Li, Yifan Li, Jianqiang Huang et al.
papers.summary: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) is essential for latency-sensitive applications. However, current causal systems face two coupled gaps. First, standard benchmarks fix the number of speakers at two and ignore the near-/far-field interference, reverberation, and sudden noise of real scenes. Second, high-performance causal architectures are too heavy for edge deployment. Lightweight alternatives try to reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, which offsets the savings. To address the first gap, we release RealSSA, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1–5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10–15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. To address the second gap, we propose Falcon, a causal AVTSE method. Its Separator performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder–decoder pass. We train Falcon with an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. This loss suppresses near-field leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across backbones. Falcon achieves state-of-the-art extraction quality on RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix. Compared with the causal AV-TFGridNet baseline, it cuts parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2 times, and GPU inference latency by 11.1 times. Code and demo are available at https://cslikai.cn/Falcon/.

papers.title: PlayerEmbed: Learning Behavioral Fingerprint Representations from Raw Input Sequences
papers.authors: Tobias Schneider, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Priya Tomar, Shahzeb Qamar et al.
papers.summary: Raw player input sequences in video games contain fine-grained behavior, but are high-dimensional and noisy, which makes large-scale analytics challenging. To address this, we introduce PlayerEmbed, a framework that learns compact and discriminative player embeddings using deep metric learning. Our approach uses a hybrid CNN-LSTM encoder trained on raw input sequences from 1,000 players. We evaluate the model on held-out sequences from these players and on sequences from 1,000 players entirely unseen during training to assess generalization to unseen identities. For player identification, a nearest-centroid classifier built from reference embeddings achieves strong performance, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.950 for players seen during training and 0.879 for players unseen during training. Systematically increasing the number of training players substantially improves generalization to unseen players, indicating a transition from simple fingerprinting to learning transferable behavioral patterns.

papers.title: Interpretable Singing Emotion Recognition Using Acoustic and Vocal Technique Features
papers.authors: Fotini Kiriakopoulou, Vassilis Lyberatos, Spyridon Kantarelis, Athanasios Voulodimos et al.
papers.summary: Singing emotion recognition relies predominantly on deep learning models that achieve strong performance but offer limited insight into the vocal characteristics driving emotion, of- ten overlooking the singing voice as a distinct signal. We propose an interpretable singing emotion recognition framework using a compact set of singing-specific descriptors across prosody, spec- tral features, phonetics, and vocal technique. To decode model decisions and link predictions to measurable acoustic phenomena, we employ SHAP and apply GRAD-CAM to qualitatively assess the learned representations of vocal techniques. Evaluations show that singing-specific features reduce cross-singer variability, while vocal technique descriptors provide interpretable insights into singing expression. Furthermore, out-of-domain evaluation on VocalSet reveals interesting associations between emotional expression and ground-truth technical execution. The analysis highlights vibrato and pharyngeal techniques as salient cues of emotional delivery, with SHAP indicating that vibrato is context-dependent on articulation rate. These findings emphasize the value of domain-specific features for interpretable singing emotion analysis.

papers.title: Past as State, Present as Attention: Persistent-State Blockwise Flow Matching for Long-Horizon Co-Speech Motion Generation
papers.authors: Yi Liu, Xiangyue Zhang, Jianfang Li, Jia Ma et al.
papers.summary: Co-speech motion generation remains challenging over long horizons due to the need for temporal coherence and consistent style. Existing methods typically generate long motions segment by segment, either conditioning on a short seed of recent frames, which gradually drifts, or retaining ever-longer explicit histories, which are costly to maintain and hard to learn from limited data. We trace these limitations to a key asymmetry between past and present: past motion carries slowly varying style that should be compactly summarized, whereas the current segment exhibits fast-changing local dynamics that require fine-grained modeling. This asymmetry motivates a simple Past-As-State, Present-as-Attention principle for long-horizon co-speech motion generation. Following this principle, we propose PASPA, which summarizes past history with an inter-block persistent state and models the current segment with intra-block bidirectional self-attention. We instantiate PASPA within a blockwise flow matching framework, with multi-block supervision for effective training over variable histories, prefill-decode state caching for efficient rollout, and hybrid classifier-free guidance for enhanced history and speech conditioning. Extensive public-benchmark experiments show that PASPA achieves state-of-the-art FGD performance and preserves motion style across long-sequence generation.

papers.title: RADIANT: Object-Centric Feed-Forward Global Illumination
papers.authors: Sarah Zhang, Zhiyang Dou, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Tod Jones et al.
papers.summary: Feed-forward neural renderers synthesize global illumination across novel 3D scenes without per-scene optimization or runtime ray tracing. Existing transformer-based renderers tokenize individual triangles, so self-attention scales quadratically with mesh resolution. Yet macroscopic radiative transport is governed by the underlying surface geometry and object arrangements rather than a particular mesh discretization; finer tessellation can thus inflate token counts without changing the underlying transport physics, motivating a discretization-agnostic and object-centric representation. We introduce RADIANT (RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer), an object-centric architecture for feed-forward global illumination from point inputs. By representing each object with a compact budget of 32 surface-patch tokens, RADIANT decouples attention sequence length from polygon counts. In a single network, an inter-object scene transformer models 3D radiative exchange and a view decoder renders images at target camera poses. To capture light transport without materializing O(N²) bias matrices, invariant form-factor attention embeds geometric distances and surface orientations directly into query-key dot products as SE(3)-invariant inner products weighted by learned area and material gains. For primary visibility without mesh connectivity, camera rays cross-attend scene tokens guided by depth-tested point splats in a shared spherical frame. Across a 1.03M-scene benchmark under matched model capacity, RADIANT reaches 25 dB tone-mapped PSNR in 5x fewer training steps than RenderFormer, and achieves 32.2 dB at 600k steps (+3.3 dB over RenderFormer and +7.6 dB over RenderFormer-V2). We further demonstrate the scalability of RADIANT, which completes a 512x512 forward pass of a 500-object scene in 0.83 s, with computational cost scaling with the number of objects rather than polygons.

papers.title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation
papers.authors: Siyang He, Qiqi Wang, Fan Liu, Yuncheng Huang et al.
papers.summary: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.

papers.title: TRACE: Data-Free Text Reconstruction Attacks against Approximate Unlearning in LLMs
papers.authors: Mengying Zhang, Derui Wang, Ibrahim Khalil, Bowen Liu et al.
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) face growing demands for data removal driven by regulatory compliance, copyright concerns, and privacy protection, approximate unlearning has emerged as a practical alternative to expensive full retraining. In practice, pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots are often maintained for auditing and rollback, introducing a previously overlooked side channel. This paper demonstrates that approximate unlearning in LLM can leave residual traces within model snapshots, which may be recoverable and thus enable the privacy breaches that approximate unlearning is intended to prevent. Here, we propose TRACE, a framework that reconstructs unlearned training data given access to pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots, without any data-specific prior knowledge. To achieve this, TRACE identifies a compact set of candidate tokens from embedding-level parameter differences to constrain the search space, and assembles sequences via a contrastive scoring mechanism based on the perplexity gap between the two models. A two-stage exploration-then-completion strategy enables the recovery of multiple distinct samples. Extensive experiments on various datasets, including TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, across multiple LLMs and six representative unlearning methods, demonstrate that TRACE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction. This paper exposes significant privacy risks in current LLM approximate unlearning deployments and highlights the need for defenses against parameter-difference leakage and appropriate management of model snapshot access.

papers.title: REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning
papers.authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Sridha Sridharan et al.
papers.summary: Regularisation-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods control the stability-plasticity trade-off through fixed coefficients tuned offline, independently of the continual learning objective and blind to phase-specific variations in data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity. We argue this is a fundamental mismatch and propose REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning, which treats regularisation strength selection as a sequential decision problem. At each incremental phase, a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) agent observes a compact state of current performance metrics and incoming data statistics, and outputs the distillation coefficients for that phase. To respect CIL's constraint on historical data access, the policy is trained entirely on pseudo-CIL tasks constructed from the initial phase, then deployed on the incremental sequence without further adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that REDAR reduces forgetting and improves forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and that policies trained on short pseudo-task horizons transfer effectively to longer incremental runs.

papers.title: GELLI: A Generator for Experiential Language Learning Interactions
papers.authors: Danilo Symonette, Alan Y. Cheng, Taiga Ikedo, Jose Manuel Rosales Juarez et al.
papers.summary: Learning a second language requires extensive practice across situations personal to each learner, yet the most effective existing approaches — narrative situations designed around specific learning goals and delivered through media — demand substantial authoring effort, limiting practice to the scope of what was built. We present GELLI, a system that generates narrative practice worlds from a learner's goals: situated scenes with characters to converse with, support alongside the interaction, and reflection, all produced at runtime with no pre authored content. In a within-subjects study with 40 learners of Japanese, GELLI produced greater vocabulary recall and confidence than expert-authored videos targeting the same goals, with no significant difference in speaking performance. Learners turned remembered or imagined situations into experiences they could shape and learn through. Support made experimentation feel safe, while unexpected narrative developments and language suggestions gave them new possibilities to pursue beyond what they initially intended to practice.

papers.title: OpenHome: From Perception to Insight in Smart-Home Camera Videos
papers.authors: Xianglong Wang, Neil Rodrigues, Pei Guo, Yiru Fang et al.
papers.summary: Vision language models (VLMs) have been increasingly adopted in consumer smart-home camera systems to interpret recorded videos and provide insights. However, video clips captured from smart-home cameras are different from curated web videos dominating existing VLM benchmarks. Smart-home video clips often do not contain subtitles or narration and are captured from different viewing angles, under various lighting conditions, and in diverse scenarios. However, the capabilities of the model in this domain, under sparse visual signals and limited context, are not fully assessed by existing VLM benchmarks. To close this gap, we introduce OpenHome, a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating smart-home video understanding. It contains 2,254 questions on 1,118 real-world video clips and organizes 10 tasks into three capability levels. Perception evaluates visible content, Reasoning evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal relationships, and Insight evaluates subject intent, supporting evidence and appropriate homeowner responses. Based on the dataset, we describe the task design, data pipeline and evaluation protocol, and report results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 81.2% overall accuracy. Frontier closed-source models outperform open-weight models on every level. The best closed-source model leads the best open-weight model by 16.3% on Perception, 22.4% on Reasoning and 37.4% on Insight.

papers.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
papers.authors: Moumita Choudhury, Amit Sarker, Shlomo Zilberstein
papers.summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the helpful agent problem. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce FavorBench, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt CooperBench to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in FavorBench, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

papers.title: WADE: An LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection Engine for WebAssembly Applications
papers.authors: Ilaria Campestrini, Stefano Zanero, Engin Kirda
papers.summary: WebAssembly (Wasm) enables near-native performance for web applications through a portable and sandboxed execution model. However, its limited runtime protection mechanisms (e.g., the lack of stack canaries and address space layout randomization (ASLR)) leave Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks. We present WADE (WebAssembly Anomaly Detection Engine), a system that detects anomalous runtime behaviors in browser-executed WebAssembly applications. WADE monitors function-level execution traces collected under benign conditions and trains a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn the normal execution behavior of each application. At runtime, the model flags deviations from these learned patterns as potential attacks. Unlike signature-based approaches, WADE builds application-specific behavioral models, enabling detection of both known and previously unseen attacks without per-vulnerability signatures. We evaluate WADE on a dataset of 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, achieving zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video Encoders using Multi-Object Interaction Videos
papers.authors: Ayushi Mehrotra, Sai Vidyaranya Nuthalapati
papers.summary: Video encoder models are increasingly used as world models for physical AI, where a policy plans by rolling out the latent, so what physics the latent holds bounds what the agent can plan over. Moreover, existing interpretability work probes quantities belonging to a single object; the quantities that make physics relational, such as momentum transfer, restitution, and friction, are defined between bodies and have not been examined. We probe relational physics attributes in two frozen self-supervised video encoders (V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE) under two-body settings and test if they transfer across environments. Our early findings are mixed. Both encoders separate elastic from inelastic collisions reliably. V-JEPA2's own predictor is less likely to predict a collision that creates kinetic energy compared to one that loses it. Momentum-violation detection appears in only one of the two encoders, a kinetic-energy readout survives a change of environment for V-JEPA2 but not for VideoMAE, and neither model holds a friction coefficient that survives a change of geometry.

papers.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
papers.authors: Lucas Ng, Georgios Batzolis, Mark Girolami
papers.summary: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recently proposed extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We give a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error in terms of a residual component vanishing under compatibility. Next, we note that existing compatible objectives put density on velocities that are infeasible on compact manifolds. We propose an objective built from an exponential family over endpoints, with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. This manifests as a reweighting of the flow matching loss which, on constant-curvature manifolds, treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Empirically, our method recovers the correct velocity field on the test case, outperforms prior methods on high-dimensional product tori, and obtains substantial NLL improvements over prior work on two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere at moderate runtime overhead. On a large dataset of high-dimensional human poses, our method outperforms prior work according to sample-based metrics.

papers.title: Agentic AI Defense: Decode-Time Provenance Binding for MCP
papers.authors: Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas, Patrick Tague et al.
papers.summary: Agentic AI systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection through untrusted tool outputs. We demonstrate cross-modal trust laundering, in which instructions concealed in an email-signature image using least-significant-bit (LSB), discrete cosine transform (DCT), or metadata steganography bypass text scanners and enter a multi-agent workflow when decoded by a tool. To counter this threat, we propose decode-time provenance binding, which combines HMAC-authenticated trust labels with an MCP-maintained provenance ledger and context-taint tracking. The mechanism labels decoded content as untrusted and blocks critical tool calls influenced by that content, even when a compromised agent substitutes a valid trusted label. We evaluate the approach using a real MCP testbed with three steganographic carriers and 24 adaptive payloads. The undefended pipeline exhibits 100% attack success, while keyword and regex defenses each permit 62.5% of attacks. Our mechanism blocks all attacks (0% success), including adversarial label substitution across mediated agent boundaries. A four-component ablation validates the roles of decode marking, cryptographic authentication, lineage tracking, and sink enforcement. An audited trusted-promotion mechanism increases legitimate-task completion from 67% to 100% without compromising protection. The approach provides carrier-independent containment within fully mediated MCP execution environments. Code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: Robotic Budding: From Homogeneous Cells to Diverse Morphologies in Physical Self-Reproduction
papers.authors: Siyuan Zhang, Junyan Liu, Wanglin He, Hod Lipson
papers.summary: Physical self-reproduction in modular robots remains difficult because a robot must not only move, but also collect, align, dock, and separate modules reliably in hardware. Taking inspiration from how genetically identical cells form the varied tissues of an organism, we introduce a single standardized robotic module that combines a magnetic docking interface with two actuated joints and folds from a flat, two-dimensional configuration into three-dimensional structures. Modules of this single design can be assembled into two morphologies: a three-module "trilobite" and a five-module "seal". Using a small set of discrete motion commands, a human operator steers an assembled parent robot to dock magnetically with a sequence of spare modules, which are assembled into a second, structurally identical individual that then separates from the parent. Because the parent retains all of its original modules, this is a budding-style form of physical reproduction. Here, we report preliminary hardware demonstrations of this full process on both morphologies. We discuss the current scope of the system, including its present reliance on direct human teleoperation rather than autonomous control, and outline directions toward autonomous execution of this process and repeated validation across a larger number of independent trials.

papers.title: Not an Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy in Humanoid Robots
papers.authors: Tiffany Bao, Shangtao Li, Yifan Sun, Mengwen He et al.
papers.summary: As humanoid robots move from research laboratories toward deployment in human-centered environments such as homes, hospitals, and warehouses, safe operation around nearby people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement. Safety filters have emerged as a promising technique to address this challenge by providing mathematical guarantees that generated control actions do not result in collisions. This paper shows that these guarantees hold only when the safety parameters are configured correctly. However, correct parameter configurations are task- and environment-specific, and no general method exists to determine them across diverse deployments. As a result, safety filters shipped with humanoid robots can fail after deployment in specific scenarios. We show that attackers can exploit these failures through only normal user interactions without any additional privileges or capabilities. To demonstrate this risk, we present goal insertion attacks and develop SIREN, an automated tool that identifies vulnerable inserting goals for a given task and environment. Experimental results show that SIREN identifies attacks in all vulnerable scenarios in the SPARK dataset. Compared with a baseline approach, SIREN discovers three times as many attacks. We also show that SIREN is able to generate attacks against a real humanoid and cause it to collide while executing tasks. These results demonstrate that current safety filters introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that can cause safety violations, which reveals that existing safety mechanisms can themselves become a source of safety risk for humanoid robots.

papers.title: Input Bias Correction in Gaussian Process Regression
papers.authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Tochukwu E. Ogri, Trivikram Satharasi, Kyle Volle et al.
papers.summary: In traditional Gaussian process (GP) regression, the inputs are typically assumed to be known, and uncertainty enters only through the measurements. When scalar fields are mapped using GP regression with measurements obtained from a mobile sensor, the inputs correspond to the estimated pose of the mobile sensor. The goal in this letter is to understand how a recorded GP, trained on erroneous inputs (e.g., pose estimates from dead-reckoning), can be corrected in a numerically efficient way when better estimates of the inputs become available. In the developed bias-aware GP (Ba-GP) framework, the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient is used to propagate estimated input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections. The resulting additive covariance structure is then exploited to develop numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms. A simulation study and an indoor light-intensity mapping experiment show that Ba-GP improves predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration relative to noisy-input GP baselines, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to full GP retraining.

papers.title: Incomparable Minima in Agent Tool Authorization
papers.authors: Xin Xu
papers.summary: An agent that needs a tool needs authority to call it, and every proposal for governing that authority has to answer one question: of two grants that both let the agent finish a task, which one is smaller? Over-privilege benchmarks score agents against this answer, and permission solvers compute it. We check the question against the authorisation tables that Microsoft and Google publish, covering 22,305 Microsoft Graph endpoint bindings and 23,852 Google API methods, on tasks generated from each table's own resource structure. For 29.8-33.3% of Graph tasks and 3.2% of Google resource tasks the question has no answer, because the minimal sufficient grants form an antichain, a set of grants none of which authorises a subset of what another does. In its two main authorisation modes, Microsoft's shipped privilegeLevel rates 67.4-74.4% of these incomparable pairs equal. Google ships no such scale, so on Google we apply a reconstruction of the FORTIS privilege ladder, which rates 90.7-98.7% equal. Applying the same reconstruction to Graph attributes much of that difference to the scale rather than the corpus: its form based on the HTTP verb alone rates 92.0% of Google pairs and 89.0-92.0% of Graph pairs equal. Four risk measures (operations, writes, services reached, administrative surface) order 28.7% of incomparable Google pairs and 15.7-23.4% of Graph pairs in opposite directions, so for those pairs the ranking has no measure-independent answer. Offered pools of minimal and larger grants, 6 frontier models pick a minimal grant on 99.0% of 1,708 decisions, a grant smallest under all four measures on 66.7%, and on 22.1% a grant that another option matches or beats on every measure. We propose that benchmarks report which minimal grant an agent chose and that deployments show the alternatives to whoever approves the grant.

papers.title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
papers.authors: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
papers.summary: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site assignment and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.

papers.title: Silence Is Not Assurance: When Production Lane Keeping Assist Does Not Warn, and What It Costs
papers.authors: Tianjia Yang, Yuxin Ding, Ke Li, Kaidi Liang et al.
papers.summary: Production lane keeping assist (LKA) systems tell the driver whether they detect the lane markings, but whether this displayed status reflects what the system perceives, and what happens when it does not, has not been examined in real-world driving. This study introduces CANDID-LKA, a CAN-based Diagnosis of the Indicated Detection status in LKA. It evaluates a proprietary driver-facing status using three signals: the displayed status and the steering torque of the driver, both recorded from the controller area network (CAN) bus of the vehicle, and the lane perception confidence of a third-party vision system observing the same road. The framework examines how the status responds to driving conditions and estimates how completely it reports degraded lane perception by comparing it with the other two signals in a latent-class model. We apply it to 39,800 seconds of real-world driving from 13 vehicle models of three manufacturers. The results show that the status does not respond consistently to the conditions that make markings harder to see, and that the three makes differ widely in how often they report not detected. The latent-class model shows that the displayed status is incomplete: it reports only 47% of degraded seconds as not detected, compared with 80% for the third-party low perception confidence, and in half of the low-confidence episodes it never reports not detected. In the silent seconds in which the status reads detected while the perception confidence is low and the driver is not in control, the standard deviation of lateral position over the next 3 s is about 60% larger than when the status and the perception confidence agree. A detected status thus does not guarantee reliable lane perception, and silence with the driver not in control is the case that most needs attention.

papers.title: Knowing When to Stop: The Evidence-Action Gap in Coding Agents
papers.authors: Tianyu Chen, Xinran Zhao, Vijay Viswanathan, Shoubin Yu et al.
papers.summary: Coding agents are trained to complete tasks, and they keep trying even when the environment makes completion impossible. The evidence that only outside help can restore progress usually appears within a few steps, yet agents rarely act on it: they over-persist, attempt undesired workarounds, and claim success the record does not support – a phenomenon we call evidence-action gap. To measure it, we introduce ImpasseBench, which injects twelve realistic environment blockers into otherwise solvable repair tasks and marks, in each trajectory, the step at which the collected evidence becomes sufficient. Scoring actions relative to that step separates appropriate effort from over-persistence and premature handoff. Across eight frontier models and 19,371 trajectories, we find that nearly every run that needs outside help collects sufficient evidence, yet a third still exhaust their budget, and every unsafe request we detect comes after that point. Fortunately, an escalation tool, or an external monitor for models that ignore the tool, already guards against much of this behavior: the tool cuts budget exhaustion from 34.0% to 6.7%, and the monitor nearly triples task success after environment restoration. Even then, a fired escalation is not yet a useful handoff: tickets reliably name the blocker but often omit the agent's own progress and verification status. Taken together, we argue that knowing when to stop therefore needs explicit support, both in the tool that lets an agent hand off and in the report it leaves behind.

papers.title: Move, don't think: sample-efficient collision avoidance with lossy proximity sensors
papers.authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan et al.
papers.summary: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.

papers.title: Emergent Cooperative Thermoregulation in Lunar Swarm Robotics
