papers.authors: Anais Jeger, Harry Holt, Lennart Puck
papers.summary: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.

papers.title: SWE-Clar: Can Coding Agents Clarify Incomplete Client Requirements and Deliver Greenfield Software?
papers.authors: Jialei Li, Dingxian Wang, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yimeng Bai et al.
papers.summary: Greenfield software development in freelance settings requires coding agents to turn incomplete client requests into working software. This makes requirement clarification essential, yet clients may be unable to provide continuous feedback over long development cycles, and receiving their answers does not guarantee correct understanding of complex requirements. These challenges motivate two benchmark design choices: clarification precedes code implementation, and its effectiveness is assessed through explicit tests of requirement understanding. Guided by these choices, we introduce SWE-Clar, a benchmark grounded in real, high-value client commissions to evaluate requirement clarification and code implementation in this setting. It comprises 100 tasks based on real software development jobs on Upwork, each with at least US4,000 in total payments. Each task begins with multi-round interaction between a coding agent and a client agent, followed by separate runs for code implementation with acceptance testing and clarification assessment. For the latter, we construct 512 questions paired with reference answers from real client-freelancer interactions, covering both explicitly stated requirements and those inferred from the conversational context. Both runs begin from the same clarification context but remain isolated, preventing assessment questions from guiding code implementation. Experiments with nine frontier models show that even GPT-6 Astra, which has the highest observed implementation score, achieves a task pass rate of only 67%, underscoring the challenge of independent software delivery in this setting. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/upwork/SWE-Clar.

papers.title: SEMPRE: Semantic-Aware Protocol Reverse Engineering via Consistency-Driven Joint Optimization
papers.authors: Yihua Xu, Weijie Huang, Xiaofeng Wang, Hang Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Protocol reverse engineering (PRE) is essential for understanding undocumented or proprietary communication formats, enabling security-critical tasks such as vulnerability discovery, malware C2 analysis, and IDS signature generation. However, existing PRE techniques rely on brittle hand-written rules, under-model contextual dependencies among neighboring fields, and often fail on messages with nested sub-protocols. We present SEMPRE, a fully automated PRE framework that replaces ad-hoc heuristics with recursive LLM reasoning grounded in fine-grained dynamic program analysis. SEMPRE uses taint-flow and loop traces to guide an LLM-driven tree-of-thought search that slices messages into fields while detecting nested sub-payloads, producing a hierarchical layout. It then infers each field's type and role and iteratively refines boundaries by freezing high-confidence segments and re-running detection under semantic constraints, yielding an EM-style procedure that monotonically improves structure and semantics until convergence. Evaluated on a broad corpus of mainstream protocols against six state-of-the-art (vs. <0.4 for all baselines) and 0.72 for semantic inference (vs. 0.13 for BinPRE). Ablations confirm the contribution of each component, and a case study on a prolific real-world botnet demonstrates practical utility.

papers.title: KVStream: Adaptive Parallel Storage Management for KV Caching in Large-Scale LLM Serving
papers.authors: Avinash Maurya, Jaiaid Mobin, Jie Ye, M. Mustafa Rafique et al.
papers.summary: Long-context LLM serving for agentic, coding, and document workloads reuses prefixes whose key-value (KV) cache outgrows GPU and host memory, putting storage I/O on the critical path of the inference step for retrieving prefixes. A single node-local NVMe absorbs all retrievals, while the parallel file system or cloud file store that nodes already mount carries almost no inference traffic. We cast prefix retrieval as aggregate-bandwidth scheduling across these tiers and present KVStream, a KV cache engine that batches a step's reads, defers writes behind the forward pass, replicates each chunk on every tier, and lets each tier adaptively claim the next unread chunks once it is free. Our performance model shows this routing attains the aggregate-bandwidth bound without prediction or tuning, whereas any static split misses it by a margin that grows as per-tier bandwidths drift or fluctuate. It also predicts that the time-to-first-token (TTFT) gain grows with load, as faster retrieval drains the queue, and disappears when host memory or arrival order keeps reuse in cache. Plugged into LMCache and evaluated on four models, six datasets, and up to 128 GPUs, KVStream retrieves within 5% of the bound, delivers up to 1.49× higher offline throughput than LMCache, and lowers mean TTFT by up to 6.1× under bursty arrivals.

papers.title: ToolContractGate: Versioned Trusted Contracts for Drift-Safe Agent Tool Invocation
papers.authors: Sachin Gupta
papers.summary: Agent tool approval and input validation do not, by themselves, bind a request to an approved source artifact. ToolContractGate provides a deterministic runtime contract evaluator for OpenAPI-derived agent tools. Each versioned ToolContract combines a stored OpenAPI fingerprint with access, schema, and behavioral declarations. The full evaluator applies ten checks, including a cached boot-time provenance result; four execution modes and five evaluation configurations support baseline, ablation, and non-blocking shadow analysis. On a synthetic benchmark of 45 cases (35 unsafe cases across 12 drift classes and 10 safe cases), the full pipeline detects all 35 faults: 29 BLOCK, 3 REVIEW, and 3 WARN decisions, with no false blocks on the safe cases. The archived run reports a mean gate latency of 0.18 ms and a 95th percentile (p95) of 2 ms using integer-millisecond measurements. The open-source artifact includes seven OpenAPI specifications, twelve enterprise contracts, 29 unit tests, and a 900-record evaluation. Results characterize contract-decision coverage; downstream enforcement requires a host that honors the returned decision. Production traffic, semantic backend drift, and dynamic provenance refresh remain evaluation and integration opportunities.

papers.title: DRAMA-Eval: A Benchmark for Context-Aware, Multi-Turn, Multi-Speaker Speech Generation
papers.authors: Jingbin Hu, Zihang Yang, Xiaoge Peng, Haoyu Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Recent advances in speech generation are shifting toward context-aware, multi-turn, and multi-speaker synthesis. While these capabilities are in high demand for applications such as audiobook and audio drama production, evaluation has not kept pace with these advances. Beyond traditional zero-shot Text-to-Speech (TTS), modern systems in this domain primarily fall into three categories: instruction-controllable generation models, multi-turn dialogue models, and the audio branches of audio-visual generation models. However, existing benchmarks evaluate these paradigms in isolation, failing to provide a unified assessment of context modeling, instruction following, and multi-speaker generation. Meanwhile, recent progress in audio understanding models has made it feasible to evaluate such complex scenarios using LLM-as-a-Judge approaches. To bridge this gap, we introduce DRAMA-Eval, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating such systems. DRAMA-Eval utilizes structured script contexts and offers a holistic evaluation framework covering objective, local, and global aspects of generation quality, enabling the assessment of acoustic fidelity, sentence-level execution, and long-range coherence. We benchmark leading open-source and commercial models on a human?verified dataset. The results reveal critical weaknesses in long-range speaker consistency and implicit instruction following that require deep contextual understanding. To facilitate reproducible research, we release a 12-hour bilingual (Chinese-English) test set of manually corrected real-world scripts, accompanied by ground-truth audio, evaluation code, and benchmark results.

papers.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
papers.authors: Wenbo Hu, Ken Li, Jiazhe Wei, Yukang Cao et al.
papers.summary: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.

papers.title: Workload-Aware Monitoring for AI-RAN
papers.authors: Babak Azkaei, Georgios Exarchakos, Kishor Chandra Joshi
papers.summary: AI-RAN platforms are expected to share CPU and GPU resources between radio workloads and AI services. Aggregate telemetry reports operating conditions, but timing changes may reflect different workloads, processors, or measurement boundaries. We propose workload-aware monitoring that associates radio-work descriptors with processing paths, timing boundaries, and operating context before comparing like with like. In 16 over-the-air downlink experiments, hybrid dispatch (CPU for transport blocks (TBs) below 4,096 bytes and GPU otherwise) has 29.66% and 22.93% lower mean host-callback durations than direct GPU dispatch, without and with a synthetic GPU co-runner, respectively. Grouping locates the separation in small TBs, while large-TB callback-duration ranges overlap. These observations identify a candidate for complementary CPU/GPU use.

papers.title: Controlled Radio Fault Injection and Telemetry Evaluation for Open 5G RANs
papers.authors: Babak Azkaei, Maxim Bîtiu, Georgios Exarchakos, Kishor Chandra Joshi
papers.summary: Radio access network (RAN) telemetry reveals radio conditions, protocol behavior, and their consequences for applications. Evaluating its usefulness requires controlled impairments and observations of the same execution. We present C and Python channel brokers and a fault injection workflow for software 5G testbeds connecting an OCUDU base station and a software UE through ZeroMQ. The brokers apply scheduled, directional transformations to I/Q samples and restore the link, while the workflow jointly records applied faults, native and programmable (codelet) telemetry, and application delay. We demonstrate this capability through 45 comparative trials of brief uplink interruptions and stepped additive noise. These use cases distinguish recognizing a radio change from measuring its service consequence: native missing-feedback events retrospectively identify interruptions, whereas noise changes decoding-error measurements without producing those events. Median on-time round-trip times remain near 30 ms, but the prespecified comparisons show mean increases in on-time 95th-percentile delay of 354 and 604 ms for one and five interruptions, and 113 ms for noise. Adding receive-side radio link control (RLC) codelet summaries did not improve interruption classification on held-out trials. The framework provides a reusable way to evaluate measurement choices under known radio faults, before using them in monitoring or learning systems.

papers.title: Signed Wasserstein distance for room impulse response comparison
papers.authors: Linda Fabiani, Sebastian J. Schlecht, Filip Elvander
papers.summary: The nature of room impulse response signals is often adverse to a clear evaluation of similarity: they are sparse, rapidly varying, signed signals resulting from the complex interaction of room reflections and phase relationships. Therefore, conventional point-wise metrics may be sensitive to small temporal shifts and provide poor loss surfaces for optimization. In this paper, we propose an optimal transport-based distance for RIR similarity that explicitly accounts for the structure of impulse responses, inspired by the signed Wasserstein distance formulation. Optimal transport provides a natural framework for this problem, by comparing signals based on how their underlying distributions are displaced rather than requiring a one-to-one correspondence. We evaluate the proposed distance against commonly used audio baseline metrics through a series of room-parameter perturbation studies. The results demonstrate the advantage of using the signed Wasserstein metric for geometric evaluation tasks and show a promising performance for room parameter optimization within a differentiable Image-Source model.

papers.title: VERA: A Responsible AI Dashboard for Assessing LLM Deployments in Light of the EU AI Act
papers.authors: Robin Quériaux, Solveig Bachellery, Léa Déléris, Saurabhsingh Rajput et al.
papers.summary: Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.

papers.title: CAMGen: A Core Change-Aware Multi-View Framework for Commit Message Generation
papers.authors: Bo Xiong, Weisheng Chen, Zongen Ren, Yifeng Zhu et al.
papers.summary: Commit messages help developers understand code changes and support software maintenance. Recent approaches use repository context to improve commit message generation (CMG) with large language models (LLMs). However, existing CMG methods provide limited support for understanding how local edits affect functionality jointly implemented by multiple code entities. This functional understanding is essential for generating commit messages that explain the main change and its impact. To address this problem, we propose CAMGen, a core change-aware multi-view commit message generation framework that incorporates functional context into generation. CAMGen identifies core entities that represent the primary change intent. It then forms candidate functional units through repository-wide semantic clustering and uses those containing the core entities to construct a Functional Semantic View. This view supplies semantic context for interpreting the affected functionality. CAMGen also uses context provided by the Structural Dependency View and the Historical Exemplar View. The context from all three views is then provided to the LLM together with the code diff to guide CMG. The experimental results show that CAMGen outperforms representative CMG baselines across three programming languages. Human evaluation further shows that CAMGen generates more complete commit messages with clearer explanations of change rationale and impact. These results demonstrate the value of functional context and complementary repository information for CMG.

papers.title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
papers.authors: Advait Gupta, Sachin Konan, Tom Yin, Gabriel Sarch et al.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

papers.title: Supporting or Replacing Students' Reasoning? Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted Proof Learning
papers.authors: Eason Chen, Sophia Judicke, Kayla Beigh, Xinyi Tang et al.
papers.summary: We studied 153 students in an undergraduate proof-based mathematics course with staggered-access to an AI support system. Students were randomly assigned to receive an AI chatbot and a homework-feedback interface earlier or later in the course. During the period when only the early-access group had access, their homework scores were 2.56 points higher, but exam performance did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that improved AI-supported homework performance did not translate into detectable gains on a subsequent exam. After all students received access, every additional 100 messages sent to the AI chatbot was associated with a 3.02-point lower score on the subsequent exam. A mediation analysis showed a significant indirect association linking lower baseline self-efficacy to greater chatbot use and, in turn, lower exam scores: a one-point decrease in self-efficacy corresponded to 0.62 fewer exam points through chatbot use. These findings raise concerns that students may use the chatbot to offload their cognitive reasoning. Use of the homework-feedback interface, which required students to submit their proof attempts before receiving feedback, was not negatively associated with exam performance. We recommend against using a chatbot for AI tutoring and suggest exploring a tutor embedded in the course activities.

papers.title: Measuring the Verifier's Floor: How Much Apparent Rare-Word Text-to-Speech Error Is ASR Error?
papers.authors: Kirill Borodin, Vasilii Kudryavtsev, Nikita Vasiliev, Grach Mkrtchian
papers.summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) is usually evaluated by transcribing its output with an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system, so the word error rate also counts recognizer errors. We measure these errors on human recordings of the test sentences. On LibriSpeech and FLEURS, the evaluation recognizer misses 33-67% of very rare words even in human speech, and all three recognizers miss 22-42%. Checking every word with two more recognizer families lowers the apparent TTS error on words that at least one recognizer hears two- to three-fold (very rare LibriSpeech words: from 10-13% to 3-5%), yet very rare words remain the hardest. Ignoring words the recognizer misses in human speech is biased: the other recognizers find TTS errors far more often on these words (4-6% vs. 0.2-0.3%) and overturn about half of the errors this mask keeps. As half of the remaining adjudicated errors may be spelling variants, a listening test is needed.

papers.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
papers.authors: Ruicong Liu, Liangyang Ouyang, Fengbo Lan, Zhixiang Wang et al.
papers.summary: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses 10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered. Project page: https://alaya-lab.github.io/AnyGameRenderer.

papers.title: How Different, or Different How? Stance Granularity in Viewpoint Selection for Dialog Systems that Engage Users with Alternative Views
papers.authors: Morita Tarvirdians, Reeve Lorena, Catharine Oertel
papers.summary: Systems that aim to help a user engage with viewpoints other than their own have to decide how different those viewpoints should be. Viewpoints are mainly represented on a scalar scale, too coarse to distinguish viewpoints that disagree with the user about different things. We introduce a selection policy in which a bandit sets how far viewpoints may sit from the user, and the policy selects the most novel viewpoint within that bound. We vary only its stance encoder, comparing a scalar score with Perspectivized Stance Vectors, which break a position into separate stances on concepts. We integrate it inside a dialog system and run a between-subjects study (N=63). Concept-level stance produces more varied exposure sequences and broader coverage of the topic's positions, but does not change how deeply users justify viewpoints or how accurately they reconstruct them. Finally, we analyze user–viewpoint relations at the concept level, showing that users reconstruct a viewpoint least accurately on concepts that one side took no position on, rather than on concepts where the two disagreed. Our findings open up opportunities for dialog systems that support engagement with alternative viewpoints by acting on which concepts a user and a viewpoint disagree on, rather than on distance alone.

papers.title: Procrustes-Bering-Sheaft: Automated Model Discovery and Virtual Crash Tests for Microservices
papers.authors: Anatoly A. Krasnovsky
papers.summary: Procrustes-Bering-Sheaft automates lightweight model discovery and virtual crash tests for microservices. Each test estimates operation availability by Monte Carlo sampling of service and communication failures. Procrustes checks deployment and tracing evidence; Bering discovers dependencies and incorporates replica declarations; Sheaft evaluates declared operation-success conditions. Independent command-line interfaces exchange reusable, versioned artifacts. The toolchain extends an earlier graph-based approach with mandatory-call contracts, failure-tolerance sweeps, baseline comparison, component-importance analysis, and CI/CD gates. We demonstrate the workflow on one HTTP operation. Six controlled execution states exposed two mismatches between reachability and observed success; an explicit required-call predicate matched all six. Two modelled one-replica additions produced different decisions: recommendation retained an availability-target violation, whereas catalog restored the baseline estimate of 0.979900 and grid tolerance of 0.12. Analytical oracles and controlled tests verify the implementation; archived replay checks numerical continuity with two earlier studies.

papers.title: PerMix: Anomalous sound detection by predicting the perturbation ratio of mixed samples
papers.authors: Jihoon Choi, Jung-Woo Choi
papers.summary: In anomalous sound detection based on self-supervised learning, the performance of the detection model largely depends on the selection of the pretext task through which the characteristics of normal data are learned. A common pretext task is to mix samples from different classes and classify the mixed sample as its target class with an angular margin loss. However, this supervision becomes mismatched when the target sample is the minority component of the mixture and the margin remains fixed irrespective of the mixing ratio. To address these issues, we propose a pretext task that directly predicts the perturbation ratio of mixed samples by reformulating the logit so that the angular margin is scaled by the perturbation ratio. In addition, we adopt a supervised contrastive loss modified for mixed samples, in which positive pairs are formed according to the dominant class. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the DCASE 2020 Task 2 benchmark. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaistss/PerMix.

papers.title: Pipelining vs. Combining in Aggregation Tasks
papers.authors: Gabriel Marques Domingues, Claire Mathieu, Boaz Patt-Shamir
papers.summary: We study the aggregation task (convergecast) in networks in the case that the values to be aggregated do not fit in a single message. We assume that every node starts with an input value, and there is an aggregation operator that is commutative, associative, and length-preserving, i.e., the result of aggregating two values has the same length as each of the input values. Since values do not fit in a message, they are transferred in a ``train'' of pipelined messages, which must be terminated whenever we want to aggregate values. The goal is to minimize the makespan time of aggregating all values. We present general lower bounds on the problem and optimal algorithms for several prevalent parallel computing architectures, including the hypercube and complete bipartite graphs, under both the splittable and unsplittable flows models. We also present an O( n) approximation for general graphs in the unsplittable flows model.

papers.title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part II: Passive Detection
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Li, Yuge Zhang, Jie Chen, Xiruo Su et al.
papers.summary: Underwater acoustic passive detection is essential to maritime surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Existing detection systems typically collapse multichannel array observations into a binary decision or a scalar confidence score, offering limited insight into the physical evidence that supports or contradicts a target declaration. This limitation is acute at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where isolated spectral peaks and transient beamforming responses are inherently ambiguous and physically verifiable targets are characterized by an ensemble of coupled reinforcing cues. Building on the unified from-signals-to-evidence framework introduced in the companion Part I, this paper instantiates the framework for passive target detection. A physics-aware multichannel acoustic encoder encodes the array observations into complementary acoustic evidence tokens through a direction-guided architecture that combines minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) processing with time-frequency and fine-frequency representations. These tokens are combined with environmental priors and fed into a pretrained large language model (LLM) that evaluates target-present and noise-only hypotheses and generates a structured detection report detailing target presence, bearing, spectral-line locations, received SNR, range, and per-field confidence scores. A physics-parameterized data engine extended to realistic oceanic channels provides traceable supervision at both discrete-label and structured-description levels. Experiments under white-noise and mixed ocean-background conditions demonstrate reliable detection, accurate bearing estimation, and physically interpretable structured reports, validating the feasibility of evidence-grounded underwater acoustic detection.

papers.title: Making Generative AI Workable at Work: Accountability, Localization, and Representation in Kenyan and Nigerian Small Businesses
papers.authors: Najeeb Gambo Abdulhamid, Stephanie Nyairo, Liz Ankrah, Jacki O'Neill
papers.summary: Generative AI is widely framed as democratizing skilled work by lowering the barrier to producing professional output. Drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with 27 workers across 21 small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in Kenya and Nigeria (July to October 2023), we find that availability alone did not make participation workable. In participants' accounts, drafting was rarely the hard part. The consequential work was making AI-assisted drafts defensible enough to circulate to clients. We identify five intertwined practices through which participants made generative AI workable: using it as draft labour, steering outputs through iterative interaction, switching and comparing across tools, performing release work to make outputs accountable before circulation, and repairing context misfit when outputs failed local requirements. We make two central contributions. First, we specify release work as a distinct, boundary-facing form of accountability labour, evidenced through verification gates, traceability reconstruction when sources fail, and non-delegation boundaries that decide what can ship. Second, we show how localization and representational failures, which we call context misfit, operate in everyday work as a recurring breakdown-and-repair class, including failures of local language, institutional knowledge, and the credible representation of African people and places, and we document the repair repertoire they demanded. Reframing democratization as workable participation, we argue that reported gains were conditional on this accountability and repair labour, and we translate the findings into four design directions for workplace generative AI. We treat Kenya and Nigeria as two situated cases, not as a representative sample of SMBs or the Global South.

papers.title: Spark-Audio 1.0 Technical Report
papers.authors: Chenyue Zhang, Cong Liu, Dingshu Tian, Dong Sun et al.
papers.summary: This paper introduces Spark-Audio 1.0, a speech foundation model trained on domestically produced computing infrastructure. The model accepts text and speech inputs and generates text outputs. It supports multilingual (99 languages) and multi-dialect (202 dialects) speech recognition, speech translation, audio perception and understanding, and both text- and speech-based dialogue, marking a shift from merely ``hearing clearly'' to genuinely ``understanding'' speech. Architecturally, Spark-Audio 1.0 couples a 0.65B-parameter dense audio encoder with a 30B-A3B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language model (LLM). The audio encoder is pretrained with representation-enhanced BEST-RQ and then refined through multi-task supervised training. The audio–LLM is trained through staged pretraining, followed by post-training that combines supervised fine-tuning with on-policy distillation. In total, the model is trained on 13 million hours of audio data together with large-scale text data. We evaluate Spark-Audio 1.0 on mainstream audio and text benchmarks, as well as on in-house test sets drawn from real-world application scenarios. Despite using substantially less audio training data than Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash, Spark-Audio 1.0 achieves comparable performance on most audio and text tasks, outperforms it in multilingual speech recognition, spoken dialogue, and real-world application scenarios, and approaches the performance of larger closed-source models. Nevertheless, there remains room for improvement in instruction following and complex audio reasoning. Finally, the successful training of Spark-Audio 1.0 on domestic hardware, including Huawei Ascend 910B and Hygon BW1000 chips, demonstrates the feasibility of a domestic technical pathway for building speech foundation models.

papers.title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
papers.authors: Timothé Picavet
papers.summary: We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed d and >0, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most d and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is d+1+, which is optimal up to for every even integer d≥ 2. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get (7+)-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and (5+)-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the 7+ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to . Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on 1/ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

papers.title: ChainSEED: A Scalable, High-Fidelity Blockchain Emulator
papers.authors: Qishu Jin, Wenliang Du, Kairui Feng
papers.summary: Researchers need blockchain experimental environments with configurable workloads, controllable network conditions, and observable outcomes. Public blockchains and testnets limit experimental control, model-based simulators omit real client implementations, and real-client environments face challenges in combining network control with resource-efficient deployment. We present ChainSEED, a scalable, high-fidelity blockchain emulator built on the SEED Internet Emulator. It separates blockchain configuration from client placement on a configurable routed network. For Ethereum PoS, it organizes separately configured execution, consensus, and validator clients and provides APIs for customizing genesis state, peer connections, and client software. A transaction generator informed by Ethereum mainnet activity, application interfaces, and chain- and node-level monitoring support experiments. ChainSEED also supports Monero and Solana. We examine beacon-node memory reduction, execution-client memory allocation, and validator-client multiplexing to support larger experiments within limited hardware budgets. On a single server with approximately 1 TiB of memory and 384 logical CPU cores, ChainSEED deploys 400 beacon nodes, 400 execution nodes, and 60,000 validator identities while sustaining approximately 20 TPS. It also emulates a 1,200-node Monero network with up to 200 active single-threaded PoW miners and a 200-node Solana network with sustained finalization. Case studies demonstrate routing attacks, blockchain amplification attacks, Monero eclipse attacks, topology-discovery benchmarking against known peer graphs, and network-configuration experiments.

papers.title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
papers.authors: Zecong Tang, Zian Guan, Yuncheng Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.

papers.title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
papers.authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Mohammad Ali Armin, Akila Pemasiri, Harshala Gammulle et al.
papers.summary: This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

papers.title: Adaptive Uncertainty Visualization With jk-Plots
papers.authors: Nikolaus Piccolotto, Daniel Pahr, Laura Lotteraner, Fatih Öztank et al.
papers.summary: An important task of uncertainty visualizations is to communicate how the number of available observations influences the precision of estimates, such as a Normal distribution's mean. In this paper, we propose an adaptive approach to visualizing univariate data that produces salient representations while highlighting the uncertainty introduced by the sample size. We introduce jk-plots, inspired by educational material of Bayesian statistics, that combine visualizations of plausible reference models (emulating popular uncertainty visualization idioms) and the observations. We describe a visualization pipeline to create jk-plots, which we implemented in an R package. We demonstrate jk-plots using synthetic datasets of varying size and discuss possible usage scenarios in domain expert interviews.

papers.title: H-2DGS: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting for Sharp and Deformable Neurosurgical Surface Reconstruction
papers.authors: Zhang Zichuan, Bart Brouwers, Rembrandt Bakker, Maud Landers et al.
papers.summary: Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29–42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.

papers.title: HimmBO: High-Dimensional Interactive Model-Merging Bayesian Optimization for Image Generation
papers.authors: Jinyuan Mao, Zhihao Shen, Chenxi Liu
papers.summary: Fine-tuning has become a common way to customize text-to-image models, leading to community collections of over 100K lightweight adapters. Adapters sharing a base model can be merged with continuous coefficients. This turns a large collection into a high-dimensional continuous design space, which recent work explores interactively using preferential Bayesian optimization (PBO). However, existing approaches are limited to a few dozen preselected adapters and require expensive image generation in every interaction round. We introduce HimmBO, a two-stage method that scales preference-driven adapter merging to much larger collections while reducing image-generation cost. Its screening stage recovers the active adapter set through level-set estimation over pre-generated images, requiring no image generation. The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.
